Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our facility with incidentally detected bilateral small solid renal and adrenal masses, a cystic mass at the head of the pancreas, and a paracaval mass. The patient was diagnosed with VHL disease and staged surgical approach was recommended based on the radiologic findings.
In the first stage, through a subcostal anterior transperitoneal approach, right adrenalectomy, resection of the paracaval mass, and enucleation for the 9 small solid renal masses were performed. A Whipple procedure was also performed to remove two smaller pancreatic lesions.
In the second stage, through an intercostal extraperitoneal approach, 5 pheochromocytomas were removed and 4 cystic renal cell carcinomas were enucleated.
After a followup of 1,5 years, the patient developed a left 1 cm renal mass, which was treated by percutaneous, ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation.
Pancreatic and adrenal functions were normal throughout the follow-up period. Blood cortisol level was 21 μg/dL upon his last control visit. There was no adrenal or extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma recurrence being detected to date.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
Surgery for right adrenalectomy, resection of the paracaval mass, enucleation of small renal masses, and Whipple procedure. Followed by surgery for removal of pheochromocytomas and enucleation of cystic renal cell carcinomas. Finally, percutaneous, ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation for the left renal mass. No replacement therapy was required for pancreatic and adrenal functions.

Follow-up:
The patient will be followed up regularly for the recurrence of renal masses, pheochromocytomas, and paragangliomas. Additionally, pancreatic and adrenal functions will also be monitored.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
**Reasoning:** The episode centred on surgical removal of VHL-associated tumours, with repeated treatment of the cystic renal cell carcinomas through enucleation and later radiofrequency ablation. Of the possible codes, the malignant kidney neoplasm takes precedence as principal diagnosis, with VHL disease (Q85.8) and pheochromocytoma as additional codes, though this choice over those alternatives is a judgement call. That places it in chapter C, category C64 (malignant neoplasm of kidney).

CODE: C64
